rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2 and 3.2, Table 3 - the authors report their own face-to-face survey of 715 Xinjiang cotton farmers and estimate a probit/double-hurdle (triple-hurdle) model of adoption willingness, adoption decision and waiting time.
rows.notes: The study does not measure any effect of water-saving or smart irrigation technology on climate adaptation, resilience or risk reduction. It analyses determinants (capital endowment, land transfer, subsidies, neighbour adoption, cooperatives) of farmers' willingness, decision and waiting time to adopt water-saving technology; the adaptation benefit of WST is asserted as a premise, not tested. Adoption is a precondition of the claimed effect, so upstream is set. Moreover, the technology studied is generic WST (the authors note over 90% of surveyed farmers use low-pressure pipe irrigation), not app-based scheduling or smart irrigation as implied by the claim's technology field. The study does state limitations (cross-sectional one-year data, omitted ease-of-use indicator) and reports standard errors, but these concern adoption determinants, not the claimed effect, so Q8 and Q9 are 'no' per rule 3.

notes: Full text appears complete (sections 1-8 plus references). The study is a socio-economic adoption study, not an evaluation of irrigation technology performance.
